title: The MOSFET as a Device
intro: A MOS transistor is a four-terminal device whose gate voltage controls a conducting channel between source and drain.

blocks.text: At the simplest level an NMOS transistor conducts between drain and source when its gate is sufficiently above its source. The gate draws no DC current because it is separated from the channel by a thin oxide, so the gate acts as a pure voltage input.

items: Source and drain: heavily doped regions (n+ for NMOS) in the substrate (p-type). The source is by definition the terminal at the lower voltage for NMOS (higher for PMOS).
Gate: a conductor (polysilicon or metal) over a thin gate oxide of capacitance Cox per unit area.
W and L: the channel width and length. The ratio W/L is the designer's main knob.
Bulk (body or substrate): usually tied to the lowest supply for NMOS and the highest for PMOS.

blocks.text: When the gate is raised far enough, electrons gather under the oxide and form an inversion layer that connects source to drain. The gate voltage at which this starts is the threshold voltage VTH.

An NMOS has an arrow pointing into the device at the source, a PMOS has an arrow out of the source. In analog schematics the bulk is often drawn explicitly. In the equations that follow NMOS quantities are positive; for PMOS the same expressions hold with all voltage and current signs reversed.

blocks.title: Switch resistance
blocks.text: An NMOS switch has mu_n*Cox = 200 uA/V^2, W/L = 20, VTH = 0.4 V and its gate is at 1.2 V. It passes a signal near 0 V. What is its on-resistance for small VDS?
solution: For small VDS the device is in the triode region, ID is about mu_n*Cox*(W/L)*(VGS - VTH)*VDS, so Ron = 1 / [mu_n*Cox*(W/L)*(VGS - VTH)].
blocks.hint: Triode region: current is linear in VDS for small VDS.
